note_claims.claim: The patient is presenting with worsening wheeze and breathlessness since yesterday.
The worsening of symptoms is associated with a viral upper respiratory infection.
The patient initially reported using salbutamol twice a day.
The patient is currently using salbutamol every two hours since last night.
The patient has experienced only brief relief from salbutamol use.
The patient is prescribed Clenil (beclometasone) 100 micrograms, two puffs twice daily.
The patient has poor adherence to the prescribed Clenil regimen.
The patient has experienced a tight chest and a small amount of clear sputum.
The patient had a fever two days ago.
The patient had one previous hospital admission three months ago for two nights.
The patient has never required intensive care or a breathing tube.
The patient is prescribed salbutamol inhaler as required.
The patient has an aspirin allergy due to bronchospasm and previously required hospital treatment.
The patient should avoid NSAIDs (like ibuprofen).
The patient's resting respiratory rate is 24.
The patient's heart rate is 108.
The patient's oxygen saturation on air is 95%.
The patient has widespread bilateral wheeze with good air entry.
The patient's peak expiratory flow (PEF) is 250 L/min.
The patient's best PEF is 450 L/min, which is about 55% of their best.
Following salbutamol nebulisation, the patient's PEF improved to 380 L/min (about 84%).
Following treatment, the patient's respiratory rate decreased to 18.
Following treatment, the patient's oxygen saturation increased to 98%.
The patient has a moderate acute asthma exacerbation triggered by a viral infection.
The patient showed a good response to the bronchodilator (salbutamol).
The patient has poor preventer adherence.
The patient is prescribed prednisolone 40 mg once daily for five days.
The patient is instructed to check inhaler technique before discharge.
The patient is scheduled for a GP or asthma nurse review within two working days.
The patient is scheduled for a GP or asthma nurse review within two working days to review inhalers and create an asthma action plan.
The patient is advised to be discharged if stable after one hour of observation.
The patient is advised to call 999 straight away if they need their blue inhaler more than every four hours, are too breathless to speak, or have blue lips.

transcript_facts.fact: Clinician observed the patient is a bit wheezy.
Patient has had a cold for a few days.
Patient's asthma has gone really bad since yesterday.
Patient is meant to take Clenil (brown preventer) twice a day.
Patient is currently using salbutamol every two hours, maybe more, since last night.
Patient is on Clenil (brown preventer).
The dose of Clenil is 100 micrograms, two puffs.
Patient was in hospital once, about three years ago, for two nights.
Patient has never needed intensive care or a breathing tube.
Patient reports a tight chest and a bit of clear phlegm.
Patient was a bit hot a couple of days ago with the cold.
Patient does not smoke but vapes every day.
Patient has an aspirin allergy (bronchospasm, previously needed hospital treatment).
Patient's breathing rate is 24, heart rate is 108, and oxygen levels are 95 percent on air.
Clinician can hear wheeze all over the patient's chest, on both sides, but air is getting in everywhere.
Patient's peak flow meter reading is 250.
Patient's best peak flow reading is about 450.
Clinician diagnoses a moderate asthma attack.
The treatment plan includes a nebuliser with salbutamol, five milligrams.
The treatment plan includes starting prednisolone 40 milligrams once a day for five days.
After nebuliser treatment, the patient's peak flow is now 380, about 84 percent of their best.
After treatment, the patient's breathing rate is 18 and oxygen is 98 percent.
The patient is instructed to use the brown inhaler every day, even when feeling well.
The patient is instructed to see their GP or asthma nurse within two working days.
Safety netting advice: Call 999 if salbutamol is needed more than every four hours, if too breathless to speak, or if lips go blue.
